topic: The Thing / Great Seal bug (Léon Theremin, Spaso House, 1945-1952)

slides.title: In 1945, Soviet schoolchildren gave the US ambassador a gift.

slides.body:
In August 1945, a group of Soviet Young Pioneers presented Ambassador Averell Harriman with a hand-carved wooden copy of the Great Seal of the United States.

He hung it in his study at Spaso House, his residence in Moscow.

Inside the carving sat a tiny device: a small metal cylinder, a paper-thin membrane and a short antenna.

No battery. No wires. Nothing to replace, and nothing to give it away.
A radio beam switched it on. Voices shook the membrane, and the bug sent the beam back, carrying the conversation with it.

slides.kicker: Built by the man behind the theremin.
slides.body:
Its designer was Léon Theremin, inventor of the eerie instrument that is played without touch.

After a decade in the US, he returned to the Soviet Union in 1938. He was imprisoned and put to work in a secret lab.

British radio operators had heard American voices on their sets, but searches came up empty.

In September 1952, a State Department technician swept the residence while the ambassador dictated. The signal led straight to the seal.

slides.kicker: Its idea is probably in your pocket.
slides.body: Because it ran on energy from an outside signal, the bug is often called a forerunner of RFID: the battery-free tags in key fobs, shop labels and contactless cards.

slides.lead: We search for threats that look like threats.
slides.accent: The real ones often arrive as gifts.

slides.line: Save this for the next gift that seems too perfect.

caption:
In 1945, Soviet Young Pioneers gave the US ambassador in Moscow a carved wooden Great Seal. Inside was The Thing, a battery-free bug designed by Léon Theremin, which listened from his study for seven years before it was found in 1952.

What's the most suspicious gift you've ever received?
